meta.title: Who really said "There comes a time in every man's life, and I've had plenty of them"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Casey Stengel really said it. But the earliest dated printing, from 1953, carries three extra words the internet drops: “at least once.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There comes a time in every man's life, and I've had plenty of them'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Stengel — but the 1953 source reads “there comes a time at least once in every man's life.” The quote cards shaved the joke.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1890–1975 · Hall of Fame outfielder and manager (Yankees, Mets)
answer.sourceLine: Stengel almost certainly said it — the Baseball Hall of Fame ↗ prints this exact short form among his own quotations. But the earliest dated printing found, a 23 August 1953 Parade item carried in Wikiquote’s sourced list ↗, reads “There comes a time at least once in every man’s life…” — and no verbatim primary transcript of the trimmed version has been located.

source.excerpt: There comes a time at least once in every man’s life, and I’ve had plenty of them.
trail: Wikiquote’s Casey Stengel page ↗ carries the line in its sourced quote list as “There comes a time at least once in every man’s life, and I’ve had plenty of them,” credited to Kevin Roberts in the 23 August 1953 issue of Parade and reproduced in “Gab with Gatts” by Art Gatts, The Lubbock Avalanche-Journal, 13 September 1953, p. 16. That is the earliest dated printing found for it.
LibQuotes ↗ records the same sentence with “at least once” shifted to after “in every man’s life,” citing Newsweek, Volume 103 (1984) and Stengel: His Life and Times (Dell, 1985), p. 252.

The trimmed form is not an internet invention: the National Baseball Hall of Fame ↗ prints “There comes a time in every man’s life, and I’ve had plenty of them” among the Stengel quotations on his Hall of Fame page, with no date or occasion attached.
Slate ↗ reports that Stengel’s gravestone reads “There comes a time in every man’s life and I’ve had plenty of them.” He is buried at Forest Lawn–Glendale ↗.
source.excerptNote: The 1953 wording as carried in Wikiquote’s sourced list. No fuller passage survives in any record found here — not the question he was answering, not the paragraph around it. What remains is the sentence, passed from Parade into a newspaper column three weeks later.
source.rightsHolder: The estate of Casey Stengel; Parade and The Lubbock Avalanche-Journal for their respective 1953 texts
source.rightsNote: This is a spoken remark, and the earliest dated printing found for it is from 1953 — well after the 1931 United States public-domain cutoff — so nothing here is public domain. Quoting a single sentence with attribution is ordinary fair use, but the 1953 Parade item and the newspaper column that reprinted it remain with their publishers, and Stengel’s own words with his estate.

author.name: Casey Stengel
author.heading: Who was Casey Stengel?
author.metaLine: 1890–1975 · Baseball Hall of Fame outfielder & manager
author.bio: Charles Dillon “Casey” Stengel played fourteen National League seasons as an outfielder before managing the New York Yankees to ten pennants and seven World Series titles — including five straight from 1949 to 1953, still the only such run — and then presiding, cheerfully, over the early New York Mets. He was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1966. What outlived the record was the voice: a looping, clause-piling, subject-losing manner that sportswriters christened Stengelese, and which threw off dozens of lines shaped exactly like this one.

misattribution.heading: Nobody stole this one — they trimmed it
misattribution.intro: No rival claimant turned up for this line, and no evidence that it belongs to anyone but Stengel. The problem is not who — it is what: the sentence in circulation has been quietly shaved.

items.who: The trimmed version on the quote cards
items.why: Aggregators print “There comes a time in every man’s life, and I’ve had plenty of them.” The oldest dated printing found — Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗, crediting Kevin Roberts in Parade, 23 August 1953 — reads “There comes a time at least once in every man’s life, and I’ve had plenty of them.” Those three words are the joke: a thing that happens at least once, of which he has had plenty.

LibQuotes ↗ carries the same three words in a different slot — “There comes a time in every man’s life at least once, and I’ve had plenty of them” — citing Newsweek, Volume 103 (1984) and Robert W. Creamer’s Stengel: His Life and Times (Dell, 1985), p. 252. Two records, two placements: what you would expect of a spoken ad-lib retold by writers rather than transcribed.

misattribution.truthLine: The name is right and the wit is his: the National Baseball Hall of Fame ↗ lists the short form among Stengel’s own quotations, and Slate ↗ reports it is the line cut into his gravestone. It is the three missing words, not the man, that got lost.

context.heading: Why the missing words matter
lead: The line is funny for one reason: it collapses in on itself. “There comes a time at least once in every man’s life” already means the thing happens to everybody, once — and then Stengel announces he has had plenty. That is the engine of Stengelese: a sentence that sets up a universal truth and then quietly runs over it. Strip out “at least once” and you still have a joke, but a blunter one.

Timing is worth noting without over-reading it. The Parade item is dated 23 August 1953, mid-season for a Yankees club that would take its fifth consecutive World Series that autumn — a run the Hall of Fame ↗ records as 1949–1953. What occasioned the remark is not stated in any record found here, so treat the date as a date, not a story.
context.detailsSummary: Why spoken lines drift like this
detailsBody: Stengel’s best-known lines were ad-libs caught by sportswriters, not text he wrote and checked. A columnist hears it, paraphrases into his own copy, another paper reprints the column, a biographer reconstructs it decades later — and each hop can lose or shift three words without anyone lying.

That is visible here in miniature: the 1953 record puts “at least once” before “in every man’s life,” while the version citing Newsweek and Robert W. Creamer’s biography puts it after. Same sentence, same speaker, two placements, and a third form — the one on the quote cards — with the phrase gone entirely.
context.pull: “At least once” is the joke. The internet deletes it and keeps the punchline.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced quote list for Casey Stengel contains "There comes a time at least once in every man's life, and I've had plenty of them," cited as quoted by Kevin Roberts in the August 23, 1953 issue of Parade and reproduced in "Gab with Gatts" by Art Gatts in The Lubbock Avalanche-Journal (September 13, 1953), p. 16.

The National Baseball Hall of Fame's Casey Stengel page lists "There comes a time in every man's life, and I've had plenty of them" among his quotations, gives his 1966 induction, his playing and managing teams, and states his Yankees were the first team to win five consecutive World Series championships, 1949-1953.

SABR's BioProject entry gives Charles Dillon Stengel, born July 30, 1890 in Kansas City, Missouri, died September 29, 1975 in Glendale, California; a .284 average over 14 National League seasons (1912-1925); managing the Yankees 1949-1960 (10 pennants, 7 World Series) and the Mets 1962-1965; and describes his rambling speaking style as "Stengelese."
LibQuotes prints "There comes a time in every man's life at least once, and I've had plenty of them," citing Newsweek, Volume 103 (1984) and Stengel: His Life and Times (Dell, 1985), p. 252.
Slate's September 2015 piece on Yogi-isms states that on Casey Stengel's gravestone it reads, "There comes a time in every man's life and I've had plenty of them."
Forest Lawn's own page states that Casey Stengel was laid to rest at Forest Lawn-Glendale as a Distinguished Resident.

Wikipedia confirms Charles Dillon "Casey" Stengel, born July 30, 1890, died September 29, 1975, Hall of Fame induction 1966, that his Yankees won the World Series for a fifth consecutive year (the only team to do so), and that his turn of phrase became known as "Stengelese."
Quote Investigator has no page investigating this quotation — a site-restricted search for the phrase returned no quoteinvestigator.com results, so no QI anchor finding exists to defer to.
